planting.note: Sow seed in winter and chill to break dormancy, then grow on and transplant small plants into short, gritty, well-drained turf or a rock garden pocket in spring; this species struggles in hot, humid summers and performs best in cool-summer climates.

directions: Grow in full sun to very light shade in short, well-drained turf or a gritty, humus-rich rock garden pocket that stays cool and evenly moist through summer; this diminutive native of Scotland's far northern coast and Orkney struggles in hot, humid summers and is best suited to cool-summer climates. Plants form tiny farina-dusted rosettes just an inch or two across and send up short stems topped with disproportionately large, deep violet-purple flowers with a bright yellow eye, typically flowering in two flushes during late spring and again in midsummer in its native habitat. Often short-lived, it is readily raised from fresh seed and is a favorite trough and rock-garden subject for alpine specialists rather than a general woodland border plant like most primroses.

planting.note: Start seed indoors with a cold stratification period and transplant young plants in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich or calcareous soil in full sun to light shade such as a streamside rock garden or damp meadow bed.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in consistently moist, humus-rich or calcareous soil such as a streamside rock garden, damp meadow bed, or bog garden margin; in the wild it favors calcium-rich flushes and damp turf across Europe's mountains and parts of northern Britain. Clusters of small, pale lilac-pink, yellow-eyed flowers open in tight, farina-dusted umbels held just above neat rosettes of narrow, mealy-backed leaves in late spring to early summer. It is one of the easier small alpine primroses for a cool, consistently damp rock garden or trough and self-sows modestly where conditions suit it.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into a sharply drained, gritty, humus-rich scree or rock garden crevice in partial shade, sited where winter wet can be kept off the crowns.

directions: Plant in a sharply drained, gritty, humus-rich scree or rock garden crevice in partial shade with protection from winter wet, ideally tucked among rocks where its roots stay cool; this species is native to limestone crevices in the Maritime Alps. Its signature feature is the fine, toothed, silvery-mealy edging on each grey-green leaf, a striking foil for the lavender-blue to violet flower clusters that open on short stems in mid-to-late spring. Long grown by alpine specialists and a parent of several garden hybrids, it is well suited to a raised bed, trough, or wall crevice where its foliage can be viewed at close range.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in a gritty, sharply drained alkaline mix, grown in a pot under glass or alpine house, or in a sheltered rock garden crevice shaded from direct summer sun and protected from winter rain.

directions: Grow in a gritty, sharply drained alkaline mix in a pot under glass or in a sheltered rock garden crevice shaded from direct summer sun and protected from winter rain, since this cushion-forming species is adapted to shaded limestone overhangs in its native Maritime Alps habitat. It forms a dense, sticky-leaved cushion that disappears under a flush of stemless, broad-faced flowers in shades of lilac-pink, rose, or white as early as midwinter to early spring, well ahead of most other primroses. Specialist alpine growers typically keep it in clay pots on a greenhouse bench or alpine house staging where humidity and moisture can be carefully controlled, since prolonged wet is its main enemy.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a pond margin, stream bank, or bog garden in partial shade, following the same culture as other Sino-Himalayan candelabra primroses.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a pond margin, stream bank, or bog garden in partial shade, following the same culture as other Sino-Himalayan candelabra primroses. Unlike the outward-facing whorls of most candelabra types, its tiered flower heads nod and turn to one side, carrying rich wine-red to magenta, heavily farina-dusted blooms on upright stems above coarse, tongue-shaped leaves in early summer. It associates well with Primula bulleyana, beesiana, and pulverulenta in a damp woodland bog planting, adding a deeper, more sculptural flower form to the candelabra primrose palette.

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant into consistently moist, humus-rich soil at a bog garden or stream margin in partial shade; allow plants to self-sow to maintain a planting since individuals are often short-lived.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil at a bog garden or stream margin in partial shade; this small Chinese candelabra primrose is shorter-lived than most of its relatives and is best maintained by letting it self-sow freely into damp, open ground each year. It produces slender stems carrying one or two tiered whorls of brilliant orange-red flowers in early summer, a vivid color unmatched by the pinks, purples, and crimsons of other candelabra species. Because individual plants often behave as biennials, it is usually grown from fresh seed and allowed to naturalize in a permanently damp woodland bog bed rather than relied upon as a long-lived clump.

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; sow in succession since plants are typically short-lived and flower heaviest in their second year before declining.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this Himalayan species flowers later than nearly all other primroses, opening its dense, flattened heads of violet-blue blooms, thickly dusted in white-yellow farina, from mid to late summer rather than spring. Because it is typically short-lived, behaving as a biennial or short-lived perennial that declines after flowering heavily, it is usually raised from fresh seed sown in succession to maintain plants in the garden. Its late bloom season and distinctive drumstick-like flower heads make it a useful extension of the primrose display into summer in a cool, moist woodland or bog garden bed.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in a gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained scree mix in partial shade or morning sun, protected from winter wet, following the same culture used for auricula and other small alpine primroses.

directions: Grow in a gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained scree mix in partial shade or morning sun, protected from winter wet, following the same alpine-house or raised-bed culture used for auricula and other small alpine primroses. 'Rufus' is a long-cultivated garden hybrid between Primula auricula and a hairy-leaved alpine relative, forming neat rosettes of soft, slightly hairy leaves topped by clusters of warm brick-red to terracotta flowers with a small pale eye in spring. It is a popular, relatively easy choice among the pubescens hybrid primroses for troughs, raised alpine beds, and rock gardens where its rich, unusual flower color stands out against more typical primrose pastels.
